extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology (readers of John Locke)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing when ideas count as true/false/right/wrong and how ideas become associated, following Locke's epistemological distinctions among simple ideas, complex ideas of substances, and complex ideas of modes/relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and falsehood properly belong to propositions, not to ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas, being bare appearances or perceptions in the mind, are not in themselves true or false; truth/falsehood properly attach to propositions (affirmations or negations) that join or separate ideas or words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An idea only becomes capable of being called true or false when the mind passes some judgment on it — i.e., tacitly or expressly affirms or denies something about it. Truth lies in joining/separating representatives (ideas or words) as the things they stand for agree or disagree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas referred to extraneous standards may be true or false
rubrics_metrics.description: When the mind refers an idea to something external (other men's ideas, real existence, or supposed real essences) the idea can be judged true or false relative to that reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three common standards of reference are: (1) conformity to the ideas in other men's minds (shared meanings of names); (2) conformity to real existence (does the idea represent something that exists); (3) conformity to the real constitution/essence of a thing. The same idea may be right in one reference and false in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas are (metaphysically) adequate copies of powers and are not false relative to real existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple ideas (sensations like blue, sweet, bitter) are the effects of powers in external objects to produce such perceptions and are therefore adequate to those powers; they cannot be false with respect to real existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because simple ideas represent only the power in things to produce certain sensations, and that power must produce that sensation, the simple idea is perfectly adequate. Differences between individuals' sensations would not render the ideas false so long as they serve as consistent distinguishing marks for use and communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas of modes and relations are archetypes and adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas formed by the mind of modes and relations (voluntary combinations of simple ideas not intended to copy any external pattern) are originals/archetypes and precisely contain what the mind intends, hence they are adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the mind itself constructs these collections of simple ideas and each complex idea contains exactly what the mind intends, such ideas cannot be inadequate in the way that ideas of substances can be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas of substances are ectypes (copies) and inherently inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas that purport to be ideas of substances are copies of external things but are necessarily imperfect and inadequate because they cannot contain all the innumerable simple ideas (powers/relations) that belong to a substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human complex ideas of substances typically abstract only a few observable powers (e.g., colour, weight, fusibility) and omit many others; since we cannot try all interactions or know all properties, our complex ideas of substances cannot be perfectly adequate or identical to the real essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: False idea: combining simple ideas never united in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex idea of a substance is false when it joins simple ideas together that, in real existence, never occur in union (e.g., a horse that barks like a dog).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such combinations, though imaginable, do not correspond to any existing species and are therefore false if judged to represent a real substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: False idea: separating by negation a simple idea consistently joined in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex idea is false when it explicitly excludes (by negation) some simple idea that in real instances is inseparably conjoined with the others (e.g., denying fixedness when fixedness accompanies other properties of gold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate negation of an inseparable property produces a false complex idea of that substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: False (or inadequate) idea: judged adequate while missing inseparable properties
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea is erroneous when one judges a complex idea to be complete or adequate for a species while it omits simple ideas that are actually inseparable in the thing (this is more inadequacy than outright falsity if no incompatible parts are joined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaving out inseparable properties leads to inadequate conception; treating such incomplete complexes as the full essence is mistaken.

rubrics_metrics.name: False idea: judged to represent the real essence
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest error is judging that a complex idea contains the real internal essence of a thing; complex ideas typically capture only some properties that flow from that essence, not the essence itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confusing observable properties with real essence leads to serious epistemic error (Locke illustrates that essences may be compact yet give rise to countless properties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas may be false in reference to other people's ideas or customary meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas (especially abstract complex ideas and mixed modes) can be considered false when they do not conform to the idea commonly signified by the same name in other people's minds or by accepted definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sort of falsity is common with mixed modes (justice, gratitude, glory) because their essences are socially constructed and the only standard available is how others use the name; disagreement produces charges of having a 'false idea.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth/falsehood presuppose judgment: right or wrong (not intrinsic to ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultimately, talk of right/wrong or true/false about ideas refers to whether the mind's tacit or explicit judgments about those ideas conform to the relevant standards (names’ meanings, real existence, essences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke recommends calling ideas 'right' or 'wrong' when measuring them against patterns; 'truth' and 'falsehood' are best reserved for propositions formed from ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association of ideas: natural correspondence vs. custom/chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas associate either by natural or proper relations (which reason should trace and maintain) or by accidental association formed through chance and custom; the latter creates habitual trains of thought that can be unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom settles habits of thinking much like bodily habits; repeated conjunctions make certain trains of ideas automatic (illustrated by musician, or by a grown person who becomes nauseated at the name of honey). These accidental associations underlie many sympathies/antipathies and contribute to persistent unreasonableness in otherwise rational minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many sympathies and antipathies arise from accidental associative links
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong likes/dislikes often originate from accidental connections of ideas (early impressions or fancies) rather than from natural constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such associations can produce strong, regular effects indistinguishable from 'natural' tendencies; awareness of their origin can aid in identifying and correcting irrational aversions or attractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names and abstracting compress knowledge but risk presuming essences
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind abstracts and names ideas to 'rank them into sorts' and hasten knowledge acquisition, but this tendency makes people prone to suppose a name carries the essence of a species, producing errors when names are assumed to reveal real essences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using names as storehouses for abstract ideas facilitates communication and reasoning, but one must be wary of tacitly assuming that an abstract idea or name equals the real essence of things.
